_what: Every sentence a client is TOLD TO TYPE into their Claude, and the tool that must answer it. Read by utils/clientPhrases.js, which stamps each phrase into its tool's description at load - so a phrase written into an email or a playbook topic cannot silently go unclaimed. Checked by tests/client-phrases.test.js.
_why: 19 Sep 2026: Guy typed 'Help me set up my LinkedHelper machine' - the exact sentence Steve Nelson's email told him to type - and got the August Windows-laptop doctrine back, answered from memory. wingguy_learn was never called, because its description claimed 'networking, outreach, LinkedIn, meetings, follow-up' and machine setup was none of those. A confident, coherent, obsolete answer that a client could not have told was wrong. This file is the reason that class of failure now fails a test instead of a client.
_rules: Add a phrase here BEFORE it goes into anything a client reads. Then run: node tests/client-phrases.test.js
phrase: exactly what the client is told to type. Matching ignores case, straight/curly quotes and trailing punctuation.
tool: the MCP tool that must answer it. The test loads that tool's real definition and checks the phrase is in its description.
topic: for wingguy_learn only - the playbook title the phrase must resolve to (a leading substring). Omit for tour phrases and 'everything'.
tour: for wingguy_learn only - 'status' or 'advance' when the phrase drives the tour rather than serving a topic.
everything: true for the phrases that mean 'read me the whole playbook'.
where: repo files that tell the client to type it. The test checks each still contains the phrase - so a doc edit that reworded it fails loudly.

near_misses: sentences NOT in any doc that a client might plausibly type, with the topic they must NOT be served ('not'), and optionally the one they SHOULD reach ('expect'). A miss is fine - it is logged as a gap and the client is told to ask Guy. The wrong topic is not.

None of this proves a client's Claude will CHOOSE the tool. It proves the description claims the words and the matcher lands them. The only proof of choice is typing the sentence into a fresh chat once before it ships - do that too.
